description: Created in 1945 to prevent war, the **UN** saves millions of lives every year, yet stays paralyzed in the face of the biggest conflicts.

hero.hook: Five countries can each block, on their own, any decision of the body meant to keep world peace.

blocks.text: The **UN**, the United Nations, was born from the ashes of the Second World War with an enormous ambition: to replace force with law. Founded in 1945, it took over from a League of Nations that had failed to prevent that second world war.

Yet from the Cold War to the tensions of today, the institution often looks powerless against the great powers. Between undeniable humanitarian successes and repeated political paralysis, the UN resembles a giant with feet of clay.

The design of the UN is not the product of a world democracy, but of a bargain between the winners of 1945. Its most powerful organ, the **[[Security Council]]**, has fifteen members, but only five of them hold real power: the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom.
The UN headquarters in New York is international territory. The billionaire John D. Rockefeller Jr. gave 8.5 million dollars to buy the land, which had previously been occupied by slaughterhouses.

These five powers hold a veto that lets a single state block any decision, even one backed by the vast majority of other countries. The mechanism was meant to stop the great powers from going to war with each other. It has become the instrument of an almost systematic paralysis: the Russian veto blocks any action on Ukraine, the American veto shields its allies in the Middle East.

The political UN is often stuck, but the operational UN wins real victories. That success rests on the **[[Specialized agencies of the UN]]**, which have their own budgets and expert staff working far from the diplomatic duels of New York.

One of the greatest achievements in human history, the eradication of smallpox in 1980, was coordinated by the World Health Organization. The World Food Programme feeds nearly 100 million people hit by famine every year.

blocks.caption: UN peacekeepers deploy to stabilize regions after a ceasefire

blocks.text: On security, the blue helmets are the visible face of UN action. Their job is not to make war but to stand between fighters after a ceasefire. Criticized after tragic failures in Rwanda and Bosnia, they remain essential for stabilizing certain areas and letting humanitarian aid through.

The fundamental limit of the UN is the principle of national sovereignty: it cannot intervene in a state's internal affairs. That principle protects countries from arbitrary meddling, but it also serves at times as a shield for dictatorships.

To close that gap, a new idea appeared in 2005: the **[[Responsibility to Protect (R2P)]]**. Under this principle, if a state fails to protect its people from mass crimes, the international community has a duty to step in. But putting it into practice still requires the agreement of the Security Council, which sharply limits its reach.
It was American president Franklin D. Roosevelt who invented the name “United Nations,” in 1942, and he put it to Winston Churchill while the British leader was in his bath.

The **[[General Assembly]]**, where every country has one vote, is still the only truly universal forum for debate. Its resolutions are not binding, but they form a powerful barometer of world opinion that even the great powers cannot entirely ignore.

The debate over reforming the UN is as old as the institution itself. Almost every diplomat admits that the current Security Council is out of date: the absence of India, Japan or any African nation among the permanent members undermines its legitimacy in much of the world.

But changing the Charter of the United Nations requires ratification by two thirds of member states, and that must include all five permanent members. None of those powers is ready to give up its veto, or even to limit it.
The veto held by the five permanent members of the Security Council has been used more than 300 times since 1945, regularly blocking any action in conflicts that touch the great powers directly.
